# AI Fashion Design, Creative Homogenization, and Copyright: Evidence, Law, and Practical Resolution

AI fashion-design tools are creating a real risk of creative convergence, but the evidence does not yet establish that they have homogenized the global fashion industry. The strongest current finding is conditional: shared models, prompts, trend data, interface defaults, and commercial optimization can make outputs more alike, especially in constrained, trend-led workflows. At the same time, AI can widen access to experimentation, generate more variations, help less-experienced creators, and support culturally specific design. A 2026 meta-analysis found a small but significant collective-homogenization effect across human–AI creative studies, while fashion-specific experiments found both increased efficiency and reduced personal-style articulation. Neither body of evidence is a representative, longitudinal study of the fashion industry.[The 2026 meta-analysis](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/0144929X.2026.2726451) [The 2026 textile-design experiment](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w)

Copyright disputes should not be framed as disputes with “the algorithm.” The legally relevant parties are independent designers and other rights holders, dataset suppliers, model developers, AI-service providers, platforms, brands, manufacturers, and users. A workable settlement requires different rules for training data, model development, generated outputs, style imitation, attribution, commercial use, and human authorship. The most practical combination is permissioned or licensed training where required, collective remuneration for mass uses, reliable provenance and records, meaningful human contribution, contractual allocation of risk, accessible takedowns and mediation, and litigation or damages for substantiated copying.

This report first defines the technology and the evidence standard, then examines adoption and named industry uses. It next tests the homogenization claim through empirical findings, mechanisms, and counterevidence. The legal analysis separates lifecycle stages and compares the United States, European Union, United Kingdom, and China before proposing a resolution package and assessing its cost, enforceability, and international limits.

## 1. Definitions, parties, and scope

### What counts as an AI fashion-design tool?

“AI fashion design” is not one technology. It describes several overlapping families of systems, and they create different creative and legal risks.

The first family is generative ideation: text-to-image, image-to-image, sketch-to-image, image-to-sketch, and text-to-video systems that produce moodboards, silhouettes, prints, colorways, campaign images, or virtual runway scenes. Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Adobe Firefly, and Runway are general-purpose examples used in fashion workflows. The fashion-specific The New Black AI is designed around garment imagery and design tasks. These systems generally produce visual proposals rather than production-ready garments.

The second family consists of design-support and workflow platforms. Cala, Yoona.ai, and similar systems may combine generative imagery with product development, trend analysis, collaboration, or supply-chain functions. Their exact architectures and training sources may not be publicly disclosed. A platform that generates a sketch is legally and commercially different from one that recommends which design is likely to sell, even if both are marketed as AI fashion tools.

The third family is forecasting, recommendation, and commercial-optimization systems. These analyze consumer behavior, social-media activity, search data, sales, and trend signals. They may not generate an image at all. They can nevertheless affect creative diversity by rewarding popular silhouettes, colors, or motifs and directing designers or suppliers toward them. Allegations concerning Shein’s algorithmic monitoring system fall primarily into this category, although the complaint also alleges that the system generated or transmitted copied design outputs.

The fourth family includes virtual try-on, garment rendering, body modeling, and digital-fashion systems. Research systems such as M2E-Try On and PAINT transfer garments onto bodies or synthesize views; they may improve visualization without originating the underlying garment concept. The Fabricant and Maison Meta operate in digital-fashion and virtual-content markets, where the output may be a digital garment, avatar asset, campaign, or competition entry rather than a physical product.

The fifth family is human–AI production tooling. A designer may use a general model only for brainstorming, then draw the garment, construct the pattern, choose materials, fit a virtual avatar, and make the physical sample manually. In that workflow, AI assists a human-authored design. Another user may accept a single generated image and sell it with little alteration. The legal and creative consequences are not equivalent.

| Tool or system | Primary function | Documented or studied fashion use | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, DALL·E, Adobe Firefly | General image generation and editing | Moodboards, concepts, visual renderings, variations, and design ideation | Outputs may be visually persuasive but often lack reliable garment construction |
| Runway | Image-to-video and text-to-video generation | Virtual fashion shows and campaign imagery | Primarily a visualization and moving-image tool |
| The New Black AI | Fashion-specific generation and editing | Text-to-image, image-to-image, sketch-related tasks, and garment variations | Benchmark evidence measures fidelity, not originality or copyright clearance |
| Cala and Yoona.ai | Fashion product-development and workflow support | Listed among tools used or emerging in fashion-company product development | Public evidence supplied here does not establish market share or model provenance |
| generative.fashion | Fashion ideation and design-space exploration | Random generation, image search, mixing, and 2D-canvas exploration | Research-interface evidence, not industry adoption |
| The Fabricant | Digital-fashion design and content production | Digital garments, virtual fashion, and brand-facing content | Vendor-reported efficiency figures lack independent validation |
| Shein’s alleged monitoring system | Trend detection, recommendation, and production optimization | Scraping and ranking of popular designs and directing supplier production | The allegations concern a company’s system, not proof of a general-purpose image model copying every output |
| M2E-Try On, PAINT, OutfitGAN and related systems | Virtual try-on, garment synthesis, and outfit matching | Body transfer, garment display, style editing, and outfit recommendation | Modeling and recommendation are not the same as originating a new fashion concept |

The distinction matters because evidence that a recommendation engine pushes popular products does not prove that a text-to-image model produces similar silhouettes. Conversely, a tool can contribute to homogenization indirectly: a generator creates many options, while a commercial-ranking system selects the few most likely to sell.

### What is creative homogenization?

Creative homogenization means a reduction in collective variation: different designers, brands, or markets repeatedly produce similar silhouettes, materials, color combinations, cultural references, body representations, or visual compositions. It does not necessarily mean that each individual designer becomes less creative, that every output is low quality, or that AI has copied a particular work.

At least five indicators can be separated:

1. **Output similarity:** AI-assisted outputs are more alike to one another than human-only outputs under comparable briefs.

2. **Reduced stylistic range:** outputs occupy a narrower range of visual or material possibilities.

3. **Repeated semantic patterns:** different users arrive at similar concepts, narratives, or references because the model supplies the same high-probability associations.

4. **Reduced representation:** bodies, cultures, materials, or aesthetics outside dominant training and market data appear less often or are rendered less accurately.

5. **Commercial convergence:** brands independently use similar trend signals, recommendation scores, and marketability criteria, causing assortments to move toward the same commercially legible designs.

These indicators should not be confused with ordinary fashion trend cycles. Fashion has always converged around seasonal silhouettes, shared cultural references, runway trends, celebrity influence, manufacturing constraints, and consumer demand. A 2023 study of more than 1.2 million K-fashion catalog images found that 43.8% were hybrid combinations of style categories, with street style the most common hybrid category at 14.3%. That study measured pre-existing market convergence, not an AI effect.[Fashion and Textiles’ K-fashion study](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40691-023-00338-8)

The relevant question is therefore not whether fashion contains similarity. It is whether AI tools add a measurable, causal layer of convergence beyond those existing forces.

### Who are the legal parties?

The algorithm is not a legal person and cannot be sued as an author, infringer, or owner. Under Chinese legal guidance, responsibility must be attributed to the provider, platform operator, deployer, application developer, or end user; autonomous operation does not itself remove human responsibility.[PRC AI intellectual-property guidance](https://practiceguides.chambers.com/practice-guides/ai-intellectual-property-2026/china/trends-and-developments)

A dispute may involve several parties at once:

- **Independent designers, artists, photographers, pattern-makers, models, and other creators** who own or claim rights in sketches, prints, photographs, patterns, technical drawings, garments, names, likenesses, or brands.
- **Rights holders and licensors** who acquired rights from creators or administer them through publishers, agencies, collective management organizations, or brands.
- **Dataset providers and curators** that assemble, label, clean, annotate, or sell training material.
- **Model developers and trainers** that collect data, train or fine-tune models, and create model weights.
- **AI-service providers and platforms** that make models available through an interface, API, marketplace, or digital-fashion service.
- **Deployers and brands** that use a model in design, marketing, recommendation, manufacturing, or retail.
- **Users and downstream manufacturers** that upload references, write prompts, select outputs, modify them, manufacture garments, or sell products.
- **Consumers and third parties** affected by false endorsement, misleading attribution, privacy violations, or counterfeit goods.

The same company can occupy several roles. A brand may be a model user, dataset owner, deployer, manufacturer, retailer, and alleged infringer. A platform may provide the model but not control a user’s final commercial output. A supplier may manufacture a copied garment while the brand selected, commissioned, or sold it. Responsibility must therefore be traced to acts and control, not assigned to an abstract “AI system.”

### Which rights are at stake?

A fashion product is a bundle of potentially separate assets:

- A sketch or illustration may be a copyright-protected artistic work.
- A textile print, embroidery, graphic, photograph, or surface pattern may receive copyright protection if it meets the jurisdiction’s originality requirements.
- A garment’s functional cut, shape, or construction may be excluded from copyright or protected through design rights or patents instead.
- A technical drawing, pattern file, specification, or sample may be protected by copyright, contract, trade-secret law, or a design right depending on the facts.
- A logo, product name, distinctive label, or source-identifying appearance may implicate trademark, trade dress, passing off, or unfair competition.
- A digital garment, avatar outfit, virtual accessory, or 3D file may fall under copyright, design, trademark, contract, or platform rules, but fashion-specific AI authority remains incomplete.
- A person’s image, voice, likeness, or recognizable persona may involve privacy, publicity, performers’ rights, passing off, or proposed personality rights rather than copyright.

This fragmentation explains why a designer may lose a copyright claim over a garment’s overall cut but still succeed over a copied print, registered design, logo, or misleading brand presentation.

## 2. Industry evidence and named examples

### Adoption is substantial but not uniform

The available adoption statistics show that fashion businesses and creative professionals are experimenting with AI, but they measure different populations and different kinds of use.

A mixed-methods study collected data from July to September 2024 through a purposive survey of 93 fashion professionals and interviews with 15 participants. Approximately 72% reported active organizational use of AI for trend forecasting, consumer analytics, and garment-design development. In the same sample, approximately 65% said AI reinforced dominant aesthetics and underrepresented non-Western cultures, minority identities, and niche fashion communities. These are self-reported perceptions, not measurements of actual output diversity or a causal estimate.[AI and Ethics fashion study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-026-01185-1)

A May 2025 Pattern Observer community survey received 174 responses from textile designers, surface-pattern designers, visual artists, and industry buyers worldwide. It reported that 73.3% used AI tools, but the breakdown is more revealing: 40.7% used AI exclusively for marketing or writing, 25.3% used it for both design and marketing, and only 7.3% used it exclusively for design and art creation. Among 125 detailed platform responses, ChatGPT was mentioned 94 times, Adobe AI tools 59 times, Midjourney 26 times, Canva AI 14 times, DALL·E 13 times, and Claude 6 times. These counts are mentions, not market shares.[Pattern Observer’s 2025 survey](https://patternobserver.com/2025/06/01/the-truth-about-ai-in-textile-design-what-174-designers-really-told-you-and-it-might-surprise-you/)

A separate account of The State of Fashion 2024 reported that 73% of fashion executives considered generative AI a business priority, while only 28% had tried it in creative design and product-development processes. The gap suggests that executive interest exceeded documented core-design experimentation in that cited sample.[European Journal of Cultural Management and Policy discussion](https://www.frontierspartnerships.org/journals/european-journal-of-cultural-management-and-policy/articles/10.3389/ejcmp.2025.13875/full)

These figures are not contradictory. A designer can use ChatGPT to write product descriptions without using an image generator for a garment. A company can make AI a strategic priority while limiting it to forecasting, customer analytics, virtual try-on, or advertising. Adoption, creative substitution, and aesthetic convergence are different variables.

### Named tools and documented applications

The following cases establish that AI fashion tools are being used in real workflows, but they do not by themselves establish homogenization.

#### Generative imagery and fashion development

Midjourney and Runway were selected for a 2023 Politecnico di Milano laboratory after an evaluation of DALL·E, Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, Adobe Firefly, and Runway. The laboratory used Midjourney for image generation, ChatGPT 3.5 for textual assistance, Runway for video generation, and CLO3D for virtual fitting. The article identifies these tools as supporting moodboards, concepts, visual renderings, and virtual fashion shows.[Politecnico di Milano laboratory](https://www.frontierspartnerships.org/journals/european-journal-of-cultural-management-and-policy/articles/10.3389/ejcmp.2025.13875/full)

The New Black AI was tested against four general-purpose systems—ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, DreamStudio, and Leonardo AI—in a 2025 study. The researchers used 450 images from the Gianfranco Ferré Research Centre’s Spring/Summer 2004 prêt-à-porter collection and 40 web-sourced fashion images. Across five tasks and 350 tests, fashion experts evaluated fidelity, accuracy, and generation errors. In free-text text-to-image tasks, the tools achieved approximately 78% fidelity for clothing and color and 65% for textiles. Guided prompts improved performance, with average scores of 80% for garment type, 77.5% for usage, and 79% for color. These are measures of reproducing requested features, not measures of originality or diversity.[Human–AI collaboration study](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI-SS/article/download/35573/37728/39644)

The same study found that The New Black AI was promising for fashion-specific image-to-image work, while ChatGPT performed better on some unstructured prompts and sketch-related tasks. It also found major limitations: the systems struggled with fabric fidelity, garment details, and converting fashion sketches into technically coherent outputs. This supports a practical distinction between visual ideation and actual fashion design. A persuasive image is not automatically a feasible pattern, construction plan, or finished garment.

The research interface generative.fashion offers a contrasting design philosophy. It allows users to generate designs randomly, upload images for search, mix designs, and explore a two-dimensional canvas whose axes can represent properties such as sleeve length, pattern, and color. It was built using StyleGAN2-ada trained on the Feidegger dataset. In qualitative and quantitative studies with fashion-design apprentices, users generally preferred it to Google Images and a text-based Stable Diffusion interface. The researchers concluded that text-only prompting restricts creative exploration, particularly for novices.[CHI study of generative.fashion](https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642908)

#### Brands, campaigns, and collaborations

The fashion industry has used generative AI in campaigns and experiments since before the current wave of mass adoption. Acne Studios explored AI with artist Robbie Barrat for its Men’s Fall/Winter 2020 collection. In 2023, Moncler, Maison Meta, and WeSayHi presented AI-generated visuals for collaborations involving Adidas Originals, Pharrell Williams, and Alicia Keys. Valentino used generative AI for a January 2023 advertising campaign for its Essential line. These examples demonstrate visibility and experimentation, but the supplied evidence does not show that they changed the brands’ underlying product-development systems or reduced design diversity.[European Journal of Cultural Management and Policy](https://www.frontierspartnerships.org/journals/european-journal-of-cultural-management-and-policy/articles/10.3389/ejcmp.2025.13875/full)

Collina Strada, Revolve, and Gucci have also been reported as using generative AI to produce fashion works, particularly silhouettes and prints. Collina Strada and other designers showed AI-assisted garments during New York Fashion Week in 2024. AWAYTOMARS and IBM Watson collaborated on novel designs. These are named use cases, not adoption rates or controlled comparisons.[Fashion copyright analysis](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/227852/11/jpaf045.pdf)

Maison Meta’s AI Fashion Week illustrates access rather than industrial substitution. A Vogue Business account reports more than 400 participants from more than 50 countries. The winning collections by José Sobral of Paatiff, Matilde Mariano of Molnm, and Opé Majek each contained 10–12 pieces and were developed into physical garments through Revolve’s Los Angeles atelier. The winners included architects and a stylist, not only conventionally trained fashion designers.[Vogue Business on the Revolve–Maison Meta drop](https://www.vogue.com/article/behind-the-scenes-of-revolves-ai-generated-drop)

The physical-production stage exposed the limits of image generation. Revolve reported that some concepts had to be “toned down” to become feasible. Opé Majek adjusted fantastical designs for comfort, function, ease, and fit. José Sobral considered construction and materials. The AI sketches were generally flat, two-dimensional views without a back, so Revolve’s teams created the missing garment structure. The case therefore shows that AI can open entry to fashion ideation while human pattern-makers, fit specialists, and product developers remain essential.

Revolve’s Mitch Moseley said the company produces roughly 6,000–8,000 designs annually and treats AI as a supplementary tool. He suggested that realistic early concepts could reduce design fallout and give development teams better direction. These are company-reported efficiency claims, not independent productivity estimates.

#### Digital fashion and vendor claims

The Fabricant’s Intelligent Tools page claims a 90% reduction in content-creation costs, an 80% increase in new design explorations, and 50–70% time savings from concept to prototype. Those figures have no stated sample, study design, or independent validation. They should be read as vendor marketing claims rather than measured industry outcomes.[The Fabricant](https://www.thefabricant.com/)

The Fabricant’s Design Forward 2026 competition offers more useful counterevidence about human signatures. FashionUnited reported 10 winners from 15 finalists, with participants from 21 countries and 45 design schools. First prize went to Tiia Jaakkola of Kolding School of Design for *Reborn Myths*, combining post-consumer denim waste, Finnish folklore, and contemporary streetwear. The jury said the strongest submissions retained the designer’s personal signature and used AI supportively.[FashionUnited on Design Forward 2026](https://fashionunited.com/education/news/the-fabricant-announces-winners-of-ai-design-forward-2026/2026051572369)

The competition cannot demonstrate that the industry is diverse overall: juried competitions select exceptional submissions. It does show, however, that AI use does not mechanically erase individual style. The workflow, data, prompts, editing, and selection practices matter.

### What the named evidence does and does not show

The named tools reveal three different adoption patterns.

First, AI is often a support technology for administrative and visual tasks. The Pattern Observer survey suggests that much reported adoption is concentrated in writing, marketing, mockups, and portfolio presentation. That use may preserve rather than replace the designer’s creative core.

Second, generative systems are increasingly involved in early-stage design. The Politecnico di Milano laboratory, the New Black AI benchmark, Maison Meta’s competition, and brand campaigns show that designers use AI for concepts, references, silhouettes, prints, and visual narratives.

Third, commercial systems increasingly connect design to forecasting, recommendation, and production. The greater the integration of AI with consumer data and rapid manufacturing, the less useful it is to examine the generated image alone. The key question becomes whether the system rewards novelty or merely identifies and reproduces whatever is already attracting attention.

The available industry evidence therefore supports adoption and experimentation, not a settled industry-wide causal conclusion. It also shows why the homogenization question must distinguish the visual generator from the recommendation and production system surrounding it.

## 3. Does AI produce creative homogenization?

### The direct empirical evidence

The strongest cross-domain evidence comes from Alwin de Rooij and Michael Mose Biskjaer’s 2026 systematic review and three-level meta-analysis. Across 19 studies and 61 effect sizes, the pooled homogenization effect was \(d = .334\), with a 95% confidence interval of [.094, .574]. The effect was statistically significant but small. Heterogeneity was substantial: \(Q(60) = 2850.50\), \(p < .001\). The review measured reduced collective diversity of meanings or artifacts, not reduced individual creativity.

The review found a crucial distinction. Human–AI co-creation often produced outputs rated as more creative, higher quality, or more enjoyable, especially among less-experienced creators. At the same time, outputs became more similar across users. Individual performance and collective diversity can therefore move in opposite directions. A tool may help a novice produce a more polished garment concept while making the entire cohort’s concepts less distinct.[de Rooij and Biskjaer’s meta-analysis](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/0144929X.2026.2726451)

The effect was task-sensitive. Homogenization was stronger in semantically constrained ideation than in minimally constrained divergent thinking. The review also found indications that convergence could persist beyond the immediate co-creative episode and appear in real-world contexts, although the included quasi-experiments were not fashion-specific and some timing information was unknown.

Fashion-specific evidence is narrower but points in the same direction. A 2026 within-subject experiment involved 34 third-year fashion-design undergraduates at a South Korean university. Each participant created 20 textile designs across ball caps, eco-bags, blankets, scarves, and sweatshirts, using both conventional vector tools and Adobe Illustrator’s generative-AI text-to-vector workflow. Eighteen participants took part in follow-up interviews.

Generative AI made idea generation easier: the mean score was 3.06 versus 2.53 in the conventional condition, with \(p = .022\). It did not significantly increase the number of ideas: the means were 2.97 versus 3.44, with \(p = .073\). The system lowered perceived task difficulty and raised perceived efficiency, but the mean score for personal-style articulation fell from 4.24 to 1.53, and editability fell from 3.91 to 2.47; both differences were statistically significant at \(p < .001\). Interviewees frequently described visually similar variations within a narrow aesthetic frame.[Fashion and Textiles experiment](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w)

This study does not prove that Adobe’s system has homogenized commercial fashion. It is an educational sample, and its outputs were not compared with a representative human-designed industry corpus. Its value is mechanistic: it shows how efficiency can coexist with less control over personal style.

A separate fashion-industry study surveyed 93 professionals and found that approximately 65% believed AI reinforced dominant aesthetics and underrepresented non-Western cultures, minority identities, and niche communities. Interview participants described repeated visual patterns and difficulty capturing local or emerging aesthetics. Because the finding is self-reported and descriptive, it measures perceived risk rather than output convergence.[AI and Ethics fashion study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-026-01185-1)

A 2026 walkthrough study of four fashion and textile design platforms found a shift from embodied techniques such as sketching and draping toward prompt-writing and linguistic precision. It reported that platforms marketed themselves as accessible and inspirational while relying on opaque infrastructures, aesthetic biases, and technical gatekeeping. The researchers warned that defaults and algorithmic suggestions could marginalize particular bodies, identities, and styles.[Platform walkthrough study](https://doi.org/10.1386/fspc_00378_1)

### Mechanism 1: concentrated and biased training data

Generative models do not learn a neutral map of all possible fashion. They learn statistical regularities from the data selected, acquired, filtered, labeled, and weighted by developers. The U.S. Copyright Office’s technical discussion explains that neural-network weights reflect patterns learned from training data and generalize them to unseen inputs. Modern generative models may require millions or billions of works, although the precise marginal value of additional data remains uncertain.[U.S. Copyright Office, Part 3](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-3-Generative-AI-Training-Report-Pre-Publication-Version.pdf)

If training data contain more images from major Western brands, commercially successful silhouettes, thin or able-bodied models, English-language descriptions, or heavily photographed fashion capitals, those patterns may become easier for the system to produce. The model need not “prefer” a culture or body type in a human sense. Its probability structure simply makes some combinations more available, legible, and technically stable than others.

A 2025 systematic review of 58 studies on cultural bias in CLIP-based text-to-image models found gender bias in 53 studies, or 91%, racial and ethnic bias in 42 studies, and other social biases in 41 studies. The review concerned text-to-image models generally, not fashion specifically, and found no fully effective mitigation strategy. Its importance for fashion is indirect but clear: a general image model can reproduce social and representational biases before it is asked to design a garment.[IEEE Access bias review](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11071263)

The review’s Stable Diffusion XL illustration generated eight samples from the prompts “a doctor” and “a nurse.” The doctors were consistently male, the nurses female, and all generated people appeared white. This is not a fashion experiment, but it demonstrates how apparently simple prompts can activate culturally patterned defaults. In fashion, the equivalent may involve assumptions about who wears a garment, what counts as a desirable body, which cultural references are “authentic,” or which materials are treated as luxurious.

Training-data concentration can also narrow material diversity. If a model sees many photographs of finished garments but relatively few technical drawings, draping experiments, unusual textiles, local craft processes, or failed prototypes, it may be better at producing familiar surface appearances than at proposing unconventional construction. The Politecnico di Milano laboratory found that its general-purpose tools lacked sufficient fashion “design language” and could not reliably translate form, body, material, volume, and geometry into construction-ready designs.

### Mechanism 2: memorization and recurring source patterns

Convergence does not always mean that a model has copied a particular designer. Diffusion systems can produce similar outputs because they learned common patterns from duplicated or highly represented sources. Technical literature summarized in the DECORAIT project reports that diffusion models can memorize content and style more than some GANs, with duplicated images and captions increasing the risk.[DECORAIT](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.14400)

Memorization creates two different problems.

The first is a copyright problem: the output may reproduce identifiable protected expression, a watermark, a print, a logo, or a substantial part of a particular work.

The second is an aesthetic-diversity problem: even without reproducing a legally protected work, the model may repeatedly draw from the same visual attractors. Many independent users can receive outputs that look alike because their prompts trigger overlapping representations of “luxury,” “minimalist,” “streetwear,” “futuristic,” or “couture.”

The difference matters legally. Copyright generally protects expression, not an abstract style, trend, technique, or genre. Similarity alone is not proof of copying. A legal system that treated every shared aesthetic as exclusive property would risk granting monopolies over ordinary fashion vocabulary and would suppress independent creation.

### Mechanism 3: shared prompts and semantic attractors

The 2026 meta-analysis describes generative AI as a “semantic attractor.” Its fluent suggestions reduce uncertainty during ideation. When many users employ similar models and exchange best-practice prompting strategies, the same attractors become shared reference points.

This mechanism is particularly plausible in fashion because designers use recurring descriptive categories: oversized, sculptural, quiet luxury, deconstructed, metallic, romantic, utilitarian, archival, sustainable, or body-conscious. Prompt templates and platform recommendations turn those categories into a limited number of highly probable visual directions.

Prompt convergence can occur even without copying. Suppose two designers ask for a “sculptural black evening dress inspired by architecture.” The model may independently generate similar asymmetrical folds, hard shoulders, or monochrome studio lighting because those elements occupy a strong region of its learned representation. The output resemblance is evidence of a common model and prompt space, not automatically evidence that one designer accessed the other’s work.

The 2025 U.S. Copyright Office report emphasizes that prompt effects remain uncertain in systems with billions of parameters. A prompt can specify a subject, theme, style, tone, or visual technique, but users often cannot predict which expressive details will be produced or omitted. This uncertainty limits human control and encourages users to accept the model’s most coherent and repeatable directions.[U.S. Copyright Office, Part 2](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-2-Copyrightability-Report.pdf)

### Mechanism 4: interface defaults and technical gatekeeping

A text-only interface gives the model considerable power to decide which visual path is easiest to produce. A user who lacks prompt fluency may repeatedly receive generic results. Even experienced users may be pushed toward the platform’s default composition, lighting, body, pose, or garment vocabulary.

The platform-walkthrough study found that prompt-writing can replace embodied design practices and that interface defaults, suggestions, and scripts influence who is recognized as a designer. This creates a form of linguistic gatekeeping: a designer’s ability to obtain distinctive results may depend less on material knowledge and more on knowing the platform’s preferred language.

The design of generative.fashion demonstrates the opposite possibility. Its canvas, image search, mixing, and random exploration tools let users navigate a visual space rather than translate every intention into words. The apprentices’ preference for that interface suggests that creative diversity depends partly on interaction design. A platform can either funnel users toward a few fluent prompt patterns or give them many ways to discover, reject, combine, and transform proposals.

Defaults also affect representation. A body model, garment template, or “standard” fit may marginalize bodies that are not well represented in the training data. A color recommendation system trained on dominant market catalogs may treat local or culturally specific combinations as less probable. Interface design therefore mediates both aesthetic diversity and cultural inclusion.

### Mechanism 5: commercial optimization and recommendation

The strongest route to industry-level convergence may not be image generation itself. It may be the connection between AI design tools and commercial feedback loops.

Fashion companies use AI for trend forecasting, consumer analytics, personalized recommendations, market analysis, virtual try-on, demand prediction, and on-demand manufacturing. These systems frequently optimize measurable outcomes such as clicks, conversion, customer retention, predicted sales, speed, or reduced production risk. If many brands optimize against similar consumer and social-media data, their design choices may converge even when the initial generative outputs differ.

The Shein class-action complaint illustrates this alleged pattern. Filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York on April 5, 2024, the complaint alleges that Shein’s system began around 2017, scraped social-media and other online sources for trending and viral designs, predicted commercial success, and sent supplier orders that changed with customer traction. It alleges thousands of products per day and, in some cases, identical copies of protected works. These are allegations, not findings, and the system described is primarily a trend-monitoring and production-optimization system rather than proof of a general-purpose generative model.[Giana v. Shein complaint](https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/24538163/shein-class-action.pdf)

The commercial mechanism is broader than copying. If a system repeatedly identifies designs that are already attracting attention, it rewards similarity to existing demand. Independent designers may be copied, but even legally independent brands may also drift toward the same high-performing visual signals. The result can be faster turnover, more frequent repetition, and less room for designs whose value is difficult to predict from immediate data.

The American Bar Association has described an earlier fast-fashion acceleration involving Shein, algorithmic trend detection, targeted advertising, online shopping, and rapid supplier recruitment. Its projection that AI could produce an “endless torrent” of designs is a forecast, not a measured result, but it identifies a real commercial risk: more design volume does not necessarily mean more diversity if selection systems favor what is already popular.[American Bar Association fashion analysis](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/intellectual_property_law/resources/landslide/2026-winter/how-will-ai-impact-fashion-industrys-public-domain/)

### Mechanism 6: human control can either widen or narrow the result

Human–AI collaboration is not one fixed process. The Politecnico di Milano laboratory identified four patterns: hierarchical, focused, random, and mutual collaboration. In hierarchical collaboration, the designer controls the process and uses AI for analysis or preliminary visualization. In focused collaboration, AI expands ideas within a designer-defined direction. In random collaboration, fragmented prompts and weak coordination produce inconsistent outputs and blind acceptance. Mutual collaboration is an ideal in which AI supports the process while the designer continually validates and adjusts results.

This framework explains why the same model can produce either more experimentation or more sameness. A designer who generates dozens of unexpected variants, rejects most of them, combines selected elements, redraws the silhouette, creates a pattern, and tests material behavior is using AI as a search space. A designer under deadline pressure who accepts the first polished result is allowing the model’s defaults to become the design language.

The South Korean textile study found that 12 participants edited post-generation results to “make the design mine again.” That response shows that personal authorship and stylistic distinction may require a second phase of human re-authoring. It also indicates a practical risk: when manual reworking is extensive, the efficiency benefit may be partly offset; when it is skipped, the design may remain within a narrow generated range.

A 2026 study of 312 Chinese designers experienced in generative-AI-assisted cultural-heritage design found that algorithmic autonomy reduced psychological ownership, while interaction transparency and interaction depth increased it. In other words, designers felt less that the result belonged to them when the system made more independent decisions, and more ownership when the interaction was understandable and iterative.[Frontiers in Psychology study](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1904639)

### Counterevidence: AI can increase experimentation and access

The homogenization hypothesis has important counterevidence.

A 2024 IEEE Access study divided 10 college students aspiring to become fashion designers into a five-person Midjourney group and a five-person control group. In three 40-minute sessions, experts rated the Midjourney group’s results higher in originality and novelty than the control group’s. Participants said AI broadened visual exploration and enabled combinations they could not find online. The sample was purposive, educational, and very small, so it cannot establish an industry effect, but it contradicts the claim that AI necessarily reduces individual novelty.[IEEE Access fashion workshop](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2024.3382194)

The same participants reported that abstract keywords could cause the system to lose direction and that it lacked sociocultural understanding and identity. One participant entered “princess and amusement park” and received a Disney-style princess despite never using the word “Disney.” This is both counterevidence and warning: AI can produce unexpected associations, but those associations may be culturally stereotyped rather than genuinely original.

The generative.fashion study found that apprentices preferred a visual exploration interface to text-only generation. Its result suggests that tools designed around divergent and convergent design practices may support more experimentation than tools that require linguistic precision.

A 2025 study built a generative model using a curated Saudi heritage database and tested more than 50 generated designs. Expert technical assessments and a visual questionnaire found that identity-informed designs significantly outperformed non-informed designs on cultural representation, attractiveness, wearability, and clarity of inspiration. Carefully curated, culturally specific data can therefore increase specificity instead of forcing a uniform global aesthetic.[Saudi heritage design study](https://doi.org/10.6007/ijarbss/v15-i5/25480)

The Politecnico di Milano laboratory also provides counterevidence. Seventy-six practitioners worked in 10 teams under the same three-outfit brief, using identical Gianfranco Ferré archival materials. The shared brief was designed to make comparison possible, yet the teams used different combinations of Midjourney, ChatGPT 3.5, Runway, prompts, commands, parameters, and human interventions. The study did not calculate a diversity score, but the teams’ differing collaboration patterns show that a shared model does not dictate a single creative pathway.

Maison Meta’s competition and The Fabricant’s Design Forward results similarly show that AI can reduce barriers to entry. Architects, stylists, and students can produce compelling proposals without following the conventional route through fashion education, studio employment, and manufacturing access. This democratization may create more voices even if the model’s raw outputs are convergent.

### What the evidence supports

The best-supported conclusion is not “AI makes fashion uniform.” It is:

> AI creates a credible, workflow-specific risk of creative homogenization, especially when many users employ the same model, prompts, datasets, defaults, trend signals, and commercial ranking criteria with limited human re-authoring. The evidence does not yet show a causal, industry-wide reduction in fashion diversity.

The risk is highest when:

- a model is trained on concentrated or culturally narrow data;
- users rely on shared prompt templates or style presets;
- the interface rewards fluent, semantically conventional descriptions;
- designers accept first-pass outputs;
- recommendation systems optimize for existing demand;
- brands use the same trend and consumer datasets;
- generated images are treated as finished designs;
- physical, cultural, body, and material diversity are not independently evaluated.

Experimentation is more likely when:

- designers use AI for divergent exploration rather than final selection;
- datasets are curated for local, cultural, body, and material diversity;
- the interface supports visual mixing and open-ended navigation;
- human experts revise, reject, and re-author outputs;
- technical prototyping tests construction and wearability;
- brands do not use marketability as the only selection criterion;
- several tools and design methods are used rather than one default model.

The largest evidence gap is representative longitudinal measurement. There is no supplied cross-brand study from 2023 through September 13, 2026 that compares AI-assisted and human-designed garments across output diversity, aesthetic similarity, cultural representation, body representation, and material diversity while separating AI effects from trend cycles, fast-fashion convergence, and selection effects. The conclusion must therefore remain qualified.

## 4. Copyright disputes involving independent designers and AI systems

### The lifecycle of a dispute

Copyright concerns arise at several different points. Treating “AI infringement” as one event obscures who acted, what was copied, and what remedy is appropriate.

| Lifecycle stage | Typical act | Potential claimant and defendant | Main legal question |
|---|---|---|---|
| Collection and preprocessing | Crawling, downloading, copying, indexing, cleaning, deduplicating, or annotating images and text | Designer or rights holder against dataset provider, trainer, developer, or platform | Was the work lawfully accessed and copied under a licence, exception, or defence? |
| Training and fine-tuning | Feeding datasets into a model and adjusting weights | Rights holder against developer, trainer, or model owner | Does training involve restricted reproduction, and do fair-use, TDM, or other exceptions apply? |
| Inference and retrieval | User uploads, retrieval-augmented generation, external search, or private fine-tuning | Rights holder against provider, deployer, platform, or user | Was protected expression copied or retrieved at the point of use? |
| Output generation | Producing a sketch, print, garment image, digital garment, or product recommendation | Rights holder against user, brand, manufacturer, platform, or provider | Does the output reproduce a substantial part of a protected work or protected design? |
| Attribution and identity | Removing a watermark, falsely naming a designer, imitating a recognizable person, or suggesting endorsement | Designer, artist, model, or brand against user, platform, or commercial seller | Are copyright, moral rights, trademark, passing off, publicity, privacy, or personality rights engaged? |
| Commercial deployment | Manufacturing, advertising, selling, licensing, or distributing the output | Rights holder against brand, retailer, supplier, or user | Who controlled the commercial act, and what damages, injunction, royalty, or account of profits is available? |

The U.K. House of Lords has described four principal stages—data collection and preprocessing, model training, inference, and output generation. At the first stage, multiple copies may be made even if the final model does not contain a human-readable copy of the original work. At the training stage, weights represent statistical patterns, but models may sometimes memorize and reproduce specific images or passages. At the output stage, the clearest infringement case is an output that reproduces a substantial part of a particular work.[House of Lords report](https://www.skadden.com/-/media/files/publications/2026/04/insights-april-2026/march-6-2026-house-of-lords-report-article-7.pdf)

### Training-data disputes

A training-data claim asks whether the developer or trainer was authorized to copy and process protected works. It is distinct from whether the final image resembles a designer’s work.

A rights holder may argue that downloading a protected image, storing it in a dataset, resizing it, indexing it, or converting it into a machine-readable form is reproduction. A developer may argue that training extracts statistical relationships rather than preserving expressive copies, that no individual work materially influences the model, or that the use is fair, transformative, or covered by a TDM exception.

The argument is fact-dependent. A model trained on lawfully licensed fashion archives is different from one trained on pirated or paywall-circumventing copies. A model that can reproduce a designer’s print or image on request presents a different risk from one that produces only generalized patterns. A system that uses retrieval at runtime may make new copies even if its foundation model was trained lawfully.

The U.S. cases illustrate the divide. As summarized in supplied legal commentary, *Bartz v. Anthropic* and *Kadrey v. Meta* held in 2025 that particular unlicensed training uses did not infringe, while *Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence* held on reconsideration that using copyrighted headnotes to train an AI system was infringement. The Ross appeal was pending. These are developing, fact-specific district-court decisions, not a universal U.S. rule.[U.S. and comparative case analysis](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/intellectual_property_law/resources/landslide/2026-winter/how-will-ai-impact-fashion-industrys-public-domain/) [EU/U.S. training analysis](https://www.stibbe.com/publications-and-insights/ai-copyright-claims-in-europe-key-considerations)

In the European Union, Article 4 of the Digital Single Market Directive permits text and data mining of lawfully accessible works for commercial and non-commercial purposes unless right holders reserve their rights in an appropriate manner, including machine-readable means for online content. Article 3 provides a stronger mandatory exception for qualifying research organizations and cultural-heritage institutions. The EU system therefore makes permission, lawful access, and the effectiveness of rights reservations central.[Directive (EU) 2019/790](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj/)

The German Munich Regional Court’s decision in proceedings involving GEMA and OpenAI was reported as holding that a model that memorizes protected works and can reproduce them in outputs goes beyond the TDM exception. The case was pending appeal, and a related CJEU reference remained unresolved as of the reporting period. The issue is not settled across the EU.[EU copyright-liability analysis](https://www.stibbe.com/publications-and-insights/ai-copyright-claims-in-europe-key-considerations)

The United Kingdom has no broad commercial TDM exception. Section 29A of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 permits copying for TDM only for non-commercial research with lawful access and, where practical, sufficient acknowledgment. The House of Lords concluded that there was no U.K. ruling specifically deciding whether commercial generative-AI training infringes, and recommended a licensing-first approach rather than a new broad exception.[House of Lords report](https://www.skadden.com/-/media/files/publications/2026/04/insights-april-2026/march-6-2026-house-of-lords-report-article-7.pdf)

China has no express statutory TDM exception for AI training, according to the supplied comparative analysis. China’s Interim Measures on the Administration of Generative AI Services require providers to use lawful training data and respect intellectual-property rights. The Supreme People’s Court’s September 7, 2026 Opinions direct courts to consider training-data sources, training-process records, model operation, the parties’ participation, preventive measures, and profits when deciding AI disputes. They improve the evidentiary framework but do not settle the copyrightability of AI-generated works.[DLA Piper comparison](https://www.dlapiper.com/en-us/insights/publications/2026/04/ai-and-copyright-major-issues-and-direction-of-travel-in-the-uk-eu-and-china-in-q2-2026/can-ai-training-result-in-copyright-infringement) [China’s Supreme People’s Court Opinions](https://chinaiplawupdate.com/2026/09/chinas-supreme-peoples-court-issues-first-national-judicial-rules-on-ai-disputes-but-sidesteps-copyrightability-of-ai-generated-works/)

### Output copying and generated-garment disputes

An output claim normally requires comparison between a protected source work and the allegedly infringing output. The claimant may need to show access, substantial similarity, copying of protected expression, and commercial use. The same-looking output can have several explanations:

- direct copying or memorization;
- retrieval of a source image at inference;
- a user’s deliberate reference image or prompt;
- common exposure to the same source;
- shared prompt vocabulary and model defaults;
- independent creation from a common trend or material;
- technical constraints that make certain forms likely.

Similarity is therefore evidence, not automatically liability.

The complaint in *Giana v. Shein* is a concrete example of the evidentiary and economic stakes. Alan Giana alleges that Shein’s algorithmic technology copied his registered artwork *Coastal Escape*, created around 2012, and displayed and sold it as a product called “Beach Print DIY Diamond Painting Without Frame.” The complaint names four Shein entities and alleges that the group’s system scraped non-Shein sources, identified commercially successful works, transmitted designs to suppliers, and sold products without authorization or attribution. It seeks class-wide damages and injunctive relief.

The complaint also alleges that one independent artist identified at least nine Shein products using her work but could not afford a lawyer. That fact is pleaded by the plaintiff, not adjudicated, but it illustrates why individual litigation is an inadequate default remedy for small designers. The supplied record does not provide a final merits judgment, class-certification decision, liability allocation, or remedy in the case.[Giana v. Shein complaint](https://s3.documentcloud.org/documents/24538163/shein-class-action.pdf)

The dispute is also not a clean example of a foundation model generating a novel garment from training data. It describes an algorithmic monitoring and production system that allegedly identifies and reproduces existing designs. That distinction is important: an AI-supported copy of a specific print is more straightforward than a new dress that merely shares a broad “quiet luxury” aesthetic.

### Style imitation is not the same as copyright infringement

Fashion designers often build commercial value through a recognizable style. A model may be prompted to produce work “in the style of” a living designer, or a platform may include artist names in a style dictionary. The output may damage commissions, reputation, or market distinctiveness even if it does not reproduce a particular copyrighted work.

Copyright generally protects expression, not style, ideas, themes, techniques, or trends. The House of Lords described this as a structural gap: AI may imitate a creator’s recognizable style without copying a substantial part of any one underlying work. It warned that protecting style through copyright could create monopolies over techniques and conventions, but recommended considering narrower protections for harmful commercial “in the style of” uses and digital replicas.[House of Lords report](https://www.skadden.com/-/media/files/publications/2026/04/insights-april-2026/march-6-2026-house-of-lords-report-article-7.pdf)

The Andersen litigation illustrates the problem. In January 2023, Sarah Andersen, Kelly McKernan, and Karla Ortiz sued Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt in the Northern District of California. The amended complaint added other artists and Runway AI, alleged 17 counts, and included copyright, trade-dress, false-endorsement, and training-data theories. It alleged that Midjourney prompt guidance recommended artist names and that a style dictionary contained approximately 4,000 artist names. Defendants disputed substantial similarity and argued that styles are not copyrightable. The case was at the pleading and amendment stage in the supplied account, not a final merits decision.[Art-law analysis of Andersen v. Stability AI](https://itsartlaw.org/art-law/artificial-intelligence-and-artists-intellectual-property-unpacking-copyright-infringement-allegations-in-andersen-v-stability-ai-ltd/) [The Fashion Law procedural account](https://www.thefashionlaw.com/court-refuses-to-dismiss-artists-copyright-claim-against-stability-ai/)

A designer who proves that a generated print reproduces identifiable protected elements has a stronger claim than one who can show only that the output “feels like” her work. Trademark, trade dress, false endorsement, passing off, unfair competition, publicity, privacy, or a new personality right may be more suitable for some style and identity harms. Each has different requirements and limits.

### Authorship and ownership of AI-assisted outputs

Authorship disputes ask who, if anyone, owns copyright in a generated image, sketch, pattern, digital garment, or collection. They are separate from whether the model’s training was lawful.

The U.S. Copyright Office’s 2023 guidance states that purely AI-generated material is not protected and that applicants must disclose more-than-de-minimis AI content, identify the human-authored elements, and exclude the AI material from the registration claim. In *Zarya of the Dawn*, the Office treated a graphic novel containing human-authored text and creative selection or arrangement as copyrightable as a whole, but not the individual Midjourney-generated images.[U.S. Copyright Office guidance](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/ai%5Fpolicy%5Fguidance.pdf)

The D.C. Circuit’s March 18, 2025 decision in *Thaler v. Perlmutter* affirmed refusal to register an image listed as autonomously created by the Creativity Machine. The court held that the Copyright Act requires a human author, although it did not decide Thaler’s waived argument that operating the machine made him the author.[D.C. Circuit decision](https://media.cadc.uscourts.gov/opinions/docs/2025/03/23-5233.pdf)

The U.S. Copyright Office’s Part 2 report says that AI used to assist rather than replace human creativity does not remove protection, but prompts alone generally do not provide sufficient control over expressive elements in currently available systems. Human contribution is assessed case by case.[U.S. Copyright Office, Part 2](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-2-Copyrightability-Report.pdf)

China has produced more varied signals. In a Beijing Internet Court judgment, a user who generated an image with Stable Diffusion was treated as the author after selecting subject matter, writing detailed positive and negative prompts, adjusting parameters, iterating, and selecting the final image. The court regarded those decisions as intellectual investment and personalized expression. The case involved downstream reuse and alleged watermark removal, not training-data liability.[Beijing Internet Court judgment](https://english.bjinternetcourt.gov.cn/pdf/BeijingInternetCourtCivilJudgment112792023.pdf)

By contrast, in *Feng v. Zhangjiagang Dongshan Cultural Communication*, the claimant created Midjourney images of artistic transparent chairs and sued over similar commercial chairs. The defendant argued that both parties used the same service and substantially similar prompts, so the similarity arose from the algorithm rather than the claimant’s originality. In March 2025, the first-instance court held that the images were not copyrightable because the claimant lacked sufficient evidence of human creative input and could not regenerate the same images from the same prompts. The appeal was dismissed in April 2025. The case shows that Chinese courts may reward detailed human control but can reject claims where process records are inadequate.[Feng v. Zhangjiagang analysis](https://www.kingandwood.com/cn/en/insights/latest-thinking/chinese-court-found-ai-generated-pictures-not-copyrightable-convergence-with-the-us-standard.html)

The supplied account of China’s September 2026 Supreme People’s Court Opinions says they do not decide whether AI-generated content is a protected “work” under the Copyright Law. The national rule remains unsettled.

The practical implication is that a designer should preserve the entire creative process: sketches, references, prompt versions, parameter settings, intermediate outputs, rejected results, edits, vector work, pattern files, material choices, fittings, and final decisions. Records cannot guarantee copyrightability, but they make human contribution and copying easier to prove.

### Attribution, commercial use, and platform terms

Attribution disputes arise when a generated output retains a watermark, uses a designer’s name, falsely suggests endorsement, or is sold without credit. Removing a watermark can be evidence of deliberate concealment, but it does not by itself establish every element of infringement.

Commercial use creates additional responsibility. A brand that sells a generated garment may be liable even if it did not train the underlying model. A model provider may face direct or secondary liability depending on its knowledge, control, inducement, and role in the specific act. A user who merely prompts a general model is less likely to be responsible for the model’s historical training than a user who fine-tunes it on another designer’s archive.

Platform terms may allocate contractual rights between provider and user, including commercial-use permissions and indemnities. They cannot normally extinguish a third-party designer’s copyright claim. A clause saying that the user owns the output is not a warranty that the output is original, non-infringing, or free from trademark, design-right, privacy, or publicity claims.

## 5. Comparative legal landscape

The four jurisdictions do not offer one shared AI-copyright rule. They overlap on the importance of human contribution and identifiable protected expression, but diverge on training exceptions, design protection, output liability, transparency, and remedies.

| Shared axis | United States | European Union | United Kingdom | China |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Human contribution | Human authorship required; AI-only material is unprotected; human selection, arrangement, editing, or other expressive control may be protected | Human originality remains the general copyright principle; AI-specific authorship law is not fully harmonized | Human-authored AI-assisted works protected; separate protection for computer-generated works under CDPA s.9(3) remains under review | Case-specific recognition where prompts, parameters, selection, and edits show personalized expression; national rule remains unsettled |
| Training data | No specific TDM statute; fair use is case-specific and U.S. decisions are divided | DSM Articles 3 and 4; lawful access, research exception, and commercial TDM subject to machine-readable reservation; AI Act adds GPAI duties | Section 29A covers non-commercial research TDM only; no broad commercial exception | No express AI-training TDM exception; lawful-data and existing copyright rules apply |
| Fashion assets | Useful articles generally excluded from copyright except separable expression; design patents, trademarks, and trade dress fill gaps | Copyright and cumulative design protection can apply; EU designs cover physical and some nonphysical products; UCD/RCD provide additional protection | Copyright, registered and unregistered design rights, trademarks, passing off, and contractual protection; garment protection is fragmented | Design patents, copyright, trademarks, trade secrets, and unfair competition; no separate AI-fashion regime |
| Output and style | Substantial similarity, fair use, copyright, Lanham Act, trade dress, and state publicity rules may apply; style alone generally weak | Copyright and design-right infringement depend on protected expression, overall impression, and national procedure; style alone is generally outside copyright | Substantial copying, design rights, trademark, passing off, privacy, and proposed personality-right routes; style gap recognized | “Access plus substantial similarity” is important; style alone is not protected, but identifiable original expression can be |
| Training transparency | No general federal disclosure rule comparable to the EU AI Act | GPAI providers must adopt copyright policies and publish training-data summaries; Article 50 requires certain output transparency from August 2, 2026 | No settled statutory training-transparency regime; reform debate continues | September 2026 judicial guidance makes training sources and process records relevant to responsibility |
| Remedies | Injunctions, actual or statutory damages, attorney fees in qualifying cases, takedowns, and class claims | National injunctions, damages, design remedies, platform procedures, and collective mechanisms vary by Member State | Injunctions, damages, account of profits, additional damages in some cases, designs and passing off; no general statutory-damages regime | Actual loss, profits, reasonable royalty, statutory damages up to RMB 5 million, possible punitive damages, and injunctions under the supplied guide |
| Main uncertainty | Fair-use treatment of training and allocation of liability across model actors | Scope of TDM reservation, memorization, extraterritoriality, and pending national/CJEU cases | Commercial training, imported models, computer-generated works, and personality rights | National copyrightability of AI output, agentic systems, training liability, and cross-border enforcement |

### The United States

#### Human authorship and fashion assets

The U.S. position begins with human authorship. *Thaler v. Perlmutter* confirms that an autonomous machine cannot be the author. The Copyright Office’s guidance allows protection for human-authored portions of AI-assisted works and for creative selections, arrangements, edits, or modifications. It does not provide a fixed threshold such as a percentage of human contribution.

Fashion designs are also limited by the useful-article doctrine. Clothing is generally a useful article, so copyright does not protect its functional shape or overall construction merely because it is attractive. Separable artistic elements—such as a graphic, surface pattern, embroidery, sculptural ornament, or illustration—may be protected. *Star Athletica v. Varsity Brands* is the central Supreme Court precedent on separability. Design patents can protect ornamental aspects of useful articles, but they require novelty and non-obviousness and can be expensive and slow for short fashion cycles. Trade dress and trademarks protect source-identifying goodwill, not a garment’s cut merely because consumers find it attractive.[ABA fashion analysis](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/intellectual_property_law/resources/landslide/2026-winter/how-will-ai-impact-fashion-industrys-public-domain/)

For an AI-assisted garment, the human designer may therefore own copyright in an original print, sketch, technical illustration, or creative arrangement while relying on design patent, trademark, or trade-dress law for other aspects. The model itself does not acquire authorship.

#### Training

The United States has no dedicated TDM exception. Fair use is evaluated case by case under purpose and character, nature of the work, amount used, and market effect. The supplied authorities show disagreement among district courts. *Bartz* and *Kadrey* favored developers on particular training claims; *Ross* favored a rights holder on the use of copyrighted headnotes. The results do not answer whether training a fashion model on a particular designer’s archive is lawful.

The U.S. debate also separates lawful acquisition from model training. In *Andersen*, artists argued that Stable Diffusion required downloading images from LAION datasets and therefore involved direct copies. Stability AI argued that the model stores parameters rather than images and does not reproduce or memorize the works in the relevant sense. The pleading-stage court left important questions unresolved.

For independent designers, the practical result is uncertainty. A provider may advertise commercial use of outputs while offering no warranty that training was licensed. A designer may have a strong claim against a copied output even if the model’s training legality remains undecided, but proving how the output was produced can be difficult.

#### Output, style, and remedies

A generated output that reproduces a particular protected print or image can support a conventional infringement claim. A general resemblance to a style usually cannot. Trademark and trade-dress claims may apply where a design or watermark creates confusion about source or affiliation. The Getty v. Stability AI litigation illustrates the difficulty of proving that an AI output containing a modified watermark creates confusion and of establishing a platform’s knowledge and control for indirect liability.[Bloomberg Industry Group analysis](https://www.insidetechlaw.com/blog/2024/05/generative-ai-in-fashion-design-complicates-trademark-ownership)

The United States offers potentially powerful remedies, including injunctions, actual damages, profits, statutory damages for qualifying registered works, and attorney fees. But litigation remains expensive. A proposed class action such as *Giana v. Shein* can address the economic reality that individual designers may not be able to litigate claims worth less than the cost of discovery. The supplied record does not establish whether that case will proceed as a class action or produce a merits remedy.

### The European Union

#### Copyright and human contribution

EU copyright law generally protects an author’s own intellectual creation. The CJEU’s *Cofemel* decision held that original clothing and footwear designs can receive copyright protection when they reflect the author’s personality; special artistic value is not required. That does not mean every garment is protected. Originality and expression remain necessary, and functionality can limit protection.[Comparative European fashion authority](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/intellectual_property_law/resources/landslide/2026-winter/how-will-ai-impact-fashion-industrys-public-domain/)

The EU has not adopted a single fully harmonized rule stating exactly how much human control is required for an AI-assisted fashion work. The general principle is favorable to a designer who makes free and creative choices, selects outputs, arranges components, modifies the result, or converts the concept into an original pattern or garment. A purely autonomous output remains doctrinally uncertain across Member States.

#### TDM and the AI Act

The DSM Directive creates a two-tier TDM framework. Article 3 provides a mandatory exception for scientific research by qualifying research organizations and cultural-heritage institutions with lawful access. Article 4 permits TDM for any purpose, including commercial purposes, when the work is lawfully accessible and the right holder has not reserved the relevant rights. For publicly available online content, the reservation should be machine-readable.

The opt-out is legally important but operationally fragile. Developers must identify the relevant signals, retain information about the source, and respect reservations across large and constantly changing datasets. The Cambridge analysis identifies unresolved questions about what counts as an appropriate reservation, whether it must be general or specific, when it must be made, and whether developers can reliably detect it.[Cambridge EU liability analysis](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/cambridge-forum-on-ai-law-and-governance/article/generative-ai-and-liability-for-copyright-infringement-under-eu-law-state-of-play-and-emerging-issues/B5D5792FBF33B8625DF530E7241005F1)

The AI Act adds obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the EU market. Article 53 requires technical documentation, a copyright policy, and a public summary of training data. The AI Act’s implementation materials state that GPAI obligations became applicable on August 2, 2025, while enforcement of relevant transparency duties is assigned to the AI Office and national authorities from August 2, 2026.[EU AI Act Article 53](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-53) [European Commission implementation materials](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai)

Article 50 applies from August 2, 2026 and requires certain providers to mark generated or manipulated synthetic content in machine-readable form and make it detectable. The Commission’s guidelines state that provider and deployer obligations can apply cumulatively to one system, including where a provider is outside the EU but its output is used in the Union. These transparency rules support attribution and accountability but do not determine copyright ownership, infringement, or remuneration.[European Commission Article 50 guidelines](https://ai.cy/images/ai-act/Transparency/Guidelines_on_the_implementation_of_the_transparency_obligations_for_certain_AI_systems_under_Article_50_of_the_AI_Act_BZptWqH0IKg1dTlDDAp41PSFY_131215.pdf)

#### Design rights and digital fashion

The 2024 EU design directive defines a design as the appearance of all or part of a product, including lines, contours, colors, shape, texture, materials, decoration, movement, transitions, and animation. Its product definition includes physical and nonphysical products such as graphic works, logos, surface patterns, typefaces, and graphical user interfaces. It allows cumulative design and copyright protection when copyright requirements are met.[Directive (EU) 2024/2823](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2024/2823/oj/eng)

The EU design system generally provides three years of unregistered Community Design protection after qualifying disclosure and registered design protection renewable for up to 25 years. Registered design protection focuses on novelty and individual character and can address products creating the same overall impression even without proving copying. The directive also recognizes that digital files or software used to reproduce a protected design can implicate design rights in 3D-printing contexts.

This makes the EU comparatively better equipped than the United States to protect short-lived fashion appearances, but the rules remain territorial and fact-specific. A virtual garment or avatar outfit may fall within the nonphysical-product language, but the supplied authorities do not establish a settled, fashion-specific AI rule for every digital asset.

#### Output liability and remedies

EU output claims may involve copyright, design rights, trademarks, unfair competition, and national procedural rules. A generated garment that reproduces protected expression can create liability even if the model’s training was lawful. A broad style resemblance ordinarily remains outside copyright, though a specific collection of expressive features may be protected.

Pending national and CJEU cases mean that the EU’s treatment of memorization, technically reproducible works, model weights, and extraterritorial training remains unsettled. The EU’s regulatory model improves documentation and market transparency, but it does not eliminate the evidentiary problem of proving which source work influenced a particular output.

### The United Kingdom

#### Existing law and unresolved reform

The United Kingdom has a narrow statutory TDM exception. Section 29A of the CDPA allows copying for non-commercial research with lawful access and, where practical, sufficient acknowledgment. The U.K. has no broad enacted exception expressly permitting commercial TDM or generative-AI training.

The CDPA also contains a distinctive rule for computer-generated works. Section 9(3) treats the author of a computer-generated work as the person who made the arrangements necessary for its creation where there is no human author. This provision has existed since 1988. The government’s March 2026 report says most respondents to its consultation supported removing protection for wholly computer-generated works while retaining protection for AI-assisted works, but no such reform had been enacted in the supplied record.[U.K. government report](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/report-and-impact-assessment-on-copyright-and-artificial-intelligence/report-on-copyright-and-artificial-intelligence)

The U.K. consultation considered four approaches: doing nothing, requiring licences in all cases, adopting a broad TDM exception, or adopting a broad exception with rights reservation and transparency. The March 2026 Impact Assessment states that there was no consensus and did not monetize the costs and benefits. It identifies the tradeoff clearly: licensing can increase remuneration and legal certainty but raise developer costs; a broad exception can reduce transaction costs and support AI development but weaken incentives to create; an opt-out system depends on technical adoption and enforcement that remain uncertain.[U.K. Impact Assessment](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/report-and-impact-assessment-on-copyright-and-artificial-intelligence/copyright-and-artificial-intelligence-impact-assessment)

The House of Lords Communications and Digital Committee recommended ruling out a new commercial TDM exception with an opt-out model, requiring statutory transparency, supporting collective licensing, and developing open provenance standards. That is a parliamentary recommendation, not enacted law.[House of Lords report](https://www.skadden.com/-/media/files/publications/2026/04/insights-april-2026/march-6-2026-house-of-lords-report-article-7.pdf)

#### Fashion protection and personality gaps

U.K. fashion protection is cumulative and fragmented. Copyright may protect sketches, textile designs, graphics, photographs, and original artistic elements. Registered and unregistered design rights can protect appearance, while trademarks and passing off protect source-identifying goodwill. A registered design generally lasts five years initially and can be renewed to 25 years. Supplementary unregistered design protection lasts three years after qualifying disclosure.

Disclosure timing creates a practical problem. A first disclosure at Paris Fashion Week may not establish U.K. unregistered protection, while a first disclosure at London Fashion Week may not establish EU unregistered protection. The status of simultaneous first disclosure remains unsettled in the supplied authority.[U.K.–EU fashion design note](https://www.murgitroyd.com/us/insights/design/how-are-fashion-designs-protected-by-intellectual-property-rights-in-the-uk-and-eu)

The U.K. lacks a general statutory personality or image right. Copyright does not protect a person merely because an AI output imitates the person’s style, voice, or persona. Passing off may assist a creator with established goodwill, but it is not a general style right. The House of Lords recommended protection against harmful commercial “in the style of” uses and unauthorized digital replicas while preserving parody, criticism, news, and other legitimate expression.

#### Enforcement and remedies

The U.K. has no general statutory-damages regime comparable to the United States. A rights holder may seek injunctions, damages, an account of profits, or additional damages in cases such as flagrant infringement, but recovery is fact-specific.
