The House of Lords emphasized that even clear output copying can be difficult to detect and expensive to litigate.

The U.K. *Getty Images v. Stability AI* proceedings show the territorial problem. Getty abandoned its primary copying claim after accepting that there was no evidence the model had been trained or developed in the United Kingdom. The court rejected a secondary claim that the imported model weights were themselves an infringing copy, and permission to appeal was granted on that novel issue. The decision did not settle whether training abroad infringes U.K. copyright or whether market-access rules can effectively regulate it.

### China

#### Human authorship and generated images

China has produced both recognition and rejection of copyright in AI-generated images. In the Beijing Internet Court case, detailed prompts, iterative changes, parameter settings, and final selection were treated as evidence of personalized human expression. In *Feng*, the court rejected copyrightability where the claimant could not prove sufficient human creative input and could not reproduce the same Midjourney result.

These decisions are final for the parties but, according to the supplied comparative review, are not binding precedents in the common-law sense. China’s Supreme People’s Court Opinions of September 7, 2026 make provenance and process records relevant to liability but do not resolve whether AI-generated content is generally a protected work.

#### Training and output responsibility

China has no express AI-training TDM exception. Existing copyright, fair-dealing, generative-AI service, and intellectual-property rules must be applied to the facts. The Guangzhou Internet Court’s February 2024 *Ultraman* decision reportedly held an AI company liable where generated images were substantially similar after unauthorized copying and adaptation. The source gives no damages figure and no fashion-specific holding.[Baker McKenzie on Chinese AI decisions](https://globallitigationnews.bakermckenzie.com/2024/05/08/china-a-landmark-court-ruling-on-copyright-protection-for-ai-generated-works/)

The September 2026 Opinions provide a more explicit output rule. If an AI user knew or should have known of a prior work, generated an output substantially similar to it, and lacked a reasonable defense, a court should support the prior rights holder’s infringement claim. The rule does not provide a quantitative similarity threshold and does not create a general right in a designer’s style.

#### Fashion assets and unfair competition

China’s ordinary IP portfolio is particularly important for fashion. A design patent can cover the appearance of all or part of a product, including shape, pattern, color, or combinations, without copyright’s separation between artistic and functional features. Public disclosure before filing can destroy novelty. Copyright can protect graphics, sketches, technical drawings, and other original works. Trademarks, trade secrets, contracts, and unfair competition provide additional routes.

The Guangzhou Internet Court’s *MO&Co* case illustrates the unfair-competition route. The court found that nearly 100 outfits, model photographs, and promotional slogans associated with the brand had been copied or imitated and ordered RMB 905,000 in damages and expenses plus a public apology. The court treated the combined conduct as misleading association even though a different trademark was used. The case did not concern generative AI, but it shows why a fashion dispute may be stronger when it combines garment imitation with copied images, slogans, presentation, and market identity.[Chinese fashion unfair-competition case](https://www.marks-clerk.com/insights/latest-insights/102jv71-china-copying-clothing-style-may-constitute-unfair-competition/)

China has no separate rules for AI-generated fashion designs, GUIs, avatars, virtual goods, or trade dress. AI involvement neither establishes nor defeats protection; ordinary design-patent, copyright, trademark, and unfair-competition requirements remain decisive.[PRC AI intellectual-property guidance](https://practiceguides.chambers.com/practice-guides/ai-intellectual-property-2026/china/trends-and-developments)

#### Remedies

The supplied PRC guide describes a graduated remedy structure: actual losses or infringer profits, then a reasonable royalty or licence fee, then statutory damages up to RMB 5 million when quantification is difficult. Wilful infringement in serious circumstances can lead to punitive damages of up to five times the base amount. Injunctions may address infringing outputs, model deployment, distribution, or training on infringing data. Litigation can seek prompts, logs, training-data sources, model operation records, filters, evaluation records, and related evidence.

This framework is promising for provenance-based disputes, but cross-border enforcement remains limited and the guide states that China lacks a comprehensive AI-specific statute.

### Cross-border conflicts

Copyright is territorial, while AI systems are global. A designer may upload work in the United Kingdom, a crawler may download it from a U.S.-hosted platform, a model may be trained in another country, an inference server may operate elsewhere, and a garment may be manufactured and sold in China, the EU, and the United States.

The EU AI Act attempts to regulate general-purpose model providers placing systems on the EU market, even where training occurred outside the Union. This can create practical market-access pressure, but it cannot automatically transform an act lawful where it occurred into infringement under every national law. The House of Lords noted the tension between extraterritorial regulation and territorial copyright.

The United Kingdom’s Impact Assessment similarly considers requiring imported models to have complied with U.K. licensing rules, but warns that developers might delay or withdraw services if compliance costs exceed the value of the market. China applies territorial IP rules and has limited cross-border enforcement of foreign judgments and injunctions. U.S. courts apply their own rules to protectability and infringement in many foreign-work disputes, and recognition of foreign judgments can vary under state law.[Comparative U.S. cross-border analysis](https://www.authorsalliance.org/2025/04/03/chinas-controversial-court-rulings-on-ai-output-and-how-it-may-affect-people-in-the-us/)

No single global rule currently answers:

- whether copying for training is authorized;
- whether a machine-readable opt-out is valid;
- whether a model weight is an infringing copy;
- how much human contribution makes an output copyrightable;
- whether a digital garment is a protected design;
- who is liable when a provider, deployer, brand, and manufacturer are in different countries;
- how an independent designer can recover a small claim across borders.

Contracts can allocate financial risk between commercial parties, but they cannot eliminate a third party’s statutory rights or guarantee recognition of a foreign injunction.

## 6. How the disputes can be resolved

A workable solution should be layered. No single measure—copyright registration, an opt-out tag, a watermark, a platform promise, or a broad training exception—can solve the full problem.

### Priority 1: separate the use cases and create a rights record

Before a designer or brand uses an AI tool, it should identify the intended use:

- business writing or marketing;
- trend forecasting or recommendation;
- visual ideation;
- image editing or variation;
- garment construction or pattern development;
- virtual try-on or body modeling;
- digital fashion or avatar assets;
- physical manufacturing and commercial sale.

The rights audit should identify the input material, the model or platform, the human decisions, the intended audience, and the commercial territory. A designer should retain dated source sketches, reference images, prompt versions, parameter settings, intermediate generations, selections, rejections, edits, vector files, pattern files, material choices, fittings, and final approvals.

This record serves several purposes. It can show that the designer created an original sketch before using AI. It can demonstrate meaningful selection and re-authoring. It can reveal whether an output was copied from a supplied reference. It can help distinguish independent creation from memorization or direct retrieval. It can also support a design-right, trade-secret, contract, or unfair-competition claim when copyright is unavailable.

Recordkeeping should be proportionate. An individual designer cannot maintain the same infrastructure as a foundation-model developer. A simple versioned folder, timestamped exports, prompt log, source register, and content-credential workflow may be enough for many projects. Brands and platforms using AI at scale should maintain stronger logs and preserve them for a defined period.

### Priority 2: license inputs by stage, purpose, and territory

Where permission is required, licensing should distinguish among:

- pretraining;
- fine-tuning;
- evaluation and testing;
- retrieval-augmented generation;
- internal search;
- display and marketing;
- generation of commercial outputs;
- physical manufacturing;
- digital-fashion distribution;
- model redistribution and downstream access.

A license for access to an image library is not automatically a license to train a foundation model, generate commercial derivatives, sublicense the model, or use an identifiable designer’s name in prompts. Contracts should specify territory, term, exclusivity, permitted models, permitted outputs, deletion or withdrawal, attribution, audit rights, remuneration, warranties, and downstream use.

For small designers, direct negotiation with a major AI developer is usually unrealistic. Collective licensing can reduce transaction costs by aggregating works, standardizing terms, collecting royalties, and administering multi-party splits. The U.K. House of Lords identified collective management organizations as important to making AI licensing accessible to individual creators and small AI firms. A 2024 Korean policy paper proposed extended collective licensing and a blockchain-based trading system, but the supplied source reports no implementation or measurable payout result.[Korean collective-licensing proposal](https://doi.org/10.30582/kdps.2024.38.2.79)

A practical licensing market could use several layers:

- direct licenses for distinctive archives, specialist datasets, or high-value fashion collections;
- collective or extended collective licenses for large catalogs where individual clearance is infeasible;
- standardized low-cost licenses for independent designers;
- revenue-sharing or royalty models for outputs or services that use licensed content;
- minimum remuneration floors and creator-first distribution rules;
- confidential audits to check whether payment reflects actual use.

No evidence supplied here proves that an existing fashion-specific collective system already reaches independent designers at scale or produces measurable payouts. That field remains unavailable. Collective licensing is a feasible institutional direction, not a demonstrated completed solution.

### Priority 3: combine transparency with provenance

Transparency must answer two different questions:

1. What kinds of data and sources did the model use?
2. Was a particular work used, and under what legal basis?

Public summaries can disclose model type, dataset categories, major sources, acquisition dates, regions, legal bases, licensed or public status, crawler types, and rights-reservation procedures. A confidential report to a regulator or trusted auditor can contain more granular information without publishing trade secrets, model weights, security-sensitive details, or every URL on the internet.

The House of Lords recommended statutory transparency duties for large developers, tailored obligations for smaller firms, and confidential disclosures modeled on the EU’s documentation approach. This is more useful than requiring a public list so long that no independent creator can read or search it.[House of Lords report](https://www.skadden.com/-/media/files/publications/2026/04/insights-april-2026/march-6-2026-house-of-lords-report-article-7.pdf)

Provenance should operate at the asset level. C2PA content credentials can record origin, creator, edits, and rights preferences. Signed metadata can be reinforced by perceptual fingerprints and invisible watermarks so that a copy can be recognized after metadata is stripped. The House of Lords described this combination as a promising “triple-lock.”[House of Lords technical-solutions chapter](https://www.skadden.com/-/media/files/publications/2026/04/insights-april-2026/march-6-2026-house-of-lords-report-article-7.pdf)

The DECORAIT prototype demonstrates a possible consent and remuneration workflow using C2PA manifests, visual fingerprinting, distributed storage, and similarity-based attribution. It tested a one-million-image corpus and up to 1,000 query images, but the authors warned that metadata can be stripped and that scalable storage remains difficult. It is a prototype, not evidence of a reliable real-world enforcement system.[DECORAIT prototype](https://arxiv.org/html/2309.14400)

Provenance is evidence, not ownership. A C2PA credential does not make an unoriginal work original, prove that a model trained on it, or prevent a platform from deleting metadata. It should therefore supplement, not replace, contracts, disclosure duties, source records, and human review.

Machine-readable rights signals such as robots.txt, TDMRep, and asset-level licensing protocols can help prevent unauthorized access. They should not be the sole protection. Site-level signals may block ordinary search along with AI crawling, may not follow a work when it is reposted, and may be ignored or circumvented. The U.K. government’s assessment and House of Lords report both identify adoption and compliance problems.

### Priority 4: define meaningful human contribution without a formula

A copyright system should not reward a designer merely for entering a short prompt, nor deny protection simply because a designer used a generative tool. The relevant question is whether human creative decisions shaped the protected expression.

For fashion, meaningful contribution may include:

- creating or materially altering the initial sketch;
- choosing and combining generated elements;
- defining the silhouette, proportions, construction, and body relationship;
- selecting materials, colors, textures, and embellishments;
- producing or materially revising a pattern;
- editing the generated image or vector output;
- rejecting alternatives and explaining the final selection;
- fitting, draping, or testing the garment;
- arranging a collection or coordinated presentation;
- writing original text, narrative, or campaign content;
- making creative decisions about the final digital or physical garment.

These factors are evidentiary, not a universal legal checklist. A technically difficult prompt is not automatically authorship, and a simple prompt followed by extensive drawing or pattern work may be significant. Courts should avoid treating prompt length as a proxy for creative control.

Designers should disclose AI assistance where a jurisdiction, platform, contract, or consumer-protection rule requires it. A clear distinction between “AI-assisted” and “wholly AI-generated” is more useful than treating all uses as equivalent. The EU’s Article 50 transparency rules concern certain synthetic content, while U.S. registration guidance requires disclosure of more-than-de-minimis AI material. These rules do not make disclosure a substitute for authorship.

Attribution should identify the human designer, collaborators, source archives where licensed, and the role of the AI tool without falsely naming the tool as a co-author or implying endorsement by a designer whose style was merely imitated.

### Priority 5: require output clearance before commercial release

A brand should not treat a provider’s commercial-use terms as a complete clearance. Before manufacturing or selling an AI-assisted garment, it should conduct proportionate checks:

- compare the output with supplied references and known source images;
- search for distinctive prints, logos, motifs, and compositions;
- inspect whether watermarks or artist names remain;
- ask whether the prompt deliberately targeted a living designer or brand;
- review the model’s known restrictions and training disclosures;
- obtain human design review;
- modify or reject outputs that appear to reproduce protected expression;
- preserve the clearance record.

Automated similarity tools can help identify near-duplicates, but they produce false positives and false negatives. A similarity score cannot decide whether a garment’s features are functional, commonplace, protected, independently created, or substantially similar in the legal sense.

The response should be graduated. If a designer identifies a plausible copy, the platform or brand should preserve logs, temporarily pause commercial distribution, remove or modify the output, notify affected suppliers, and offer attribution, a licence, a royalty, or a settlement where appropriate. Litigation should be reserved for disputed, commercially significant, repeated, or willful conduct, but the availability of a credible injunction remains important.

### Priority 6: allocate risk through contracts

Every commercial AI-fashion agreement should address:

- who owns the designer’s pre-existing material;
- whether the platform may use uploads for training or fine-tuning;
- whether the user’s work is included in a public model;
- which outputs may be used commercially;
- who owns human-authored modifications and arrangements;
- whether the provider warrants dataset compliance;
- whether the provider offers indemnity and subject to what limits;
- who investigates third-party claims;
- how logs and provenance data are preserved;
- how takedowns, redesign, refunds, and product withdrawals work;
- who pays damages, royalties, legal costs, and recall expenses;
- whether the brand may audit the provider;
- whether the contract provides mediation or arbitration;
- what law and forum govern the contract;
- what happens when a designer withdraws consent or a model is discontinued.

Brands should also bind manufacturers and suppliers to preserve source records and refrain from using unapproved AI systems. A supplier certificate saying that a product does not infringe is weak protection if the brand’s own monitoring system selected the design. Responsibility should follow control and benefit.

Independent designers should avoid broad clauses that silently transfer training, likeness, or style rights through ordinary commissioning language. Consent to photograph a garment is not necessarily consent to train a model on the photograph. Permission to use a model’s image in one campaign is not necessarily permission to create an AI replica or avatar. The 2026 Rainbow Shops litigation involving model Francheska Pujols illustrates why contracts should expressly address AI training, likeness replication, and uses beyond the original engagement; the case remained pending in the supplied account.[Rainbow Shops litigation account](https://sharmalawpllc.com/ai-models-in-fashion-what-every-contract-needs-to-say-in-2026/)

Contracts cannot prevent a third-party rights holder from suing, but they can determine who investigates, preserves evidence, pays, negotiates, redesigns, and bears the commercial loss.

### Priority 7: create affordable enforcement

The ordinary litigation model is poorly matched to independent fashion businesses. Monitoring millions of outputs is expensive, and a single copied print may not justify a federal lawsuit even when the aggregate harm is substantial.

A practical enforcement ladder should include:

1. a standardized platform notice with source files, registration or design records, URLs, dates, and comparison images;
2. rapid temporary removal or de-listing while the parties investigate;
3. disclosure of relevant prompts, source references, output logs, and supplier records;
4. attribution, licence negotiation, redesign, royalties, or settlement;
5. collective claims, representative actions, or class litigation where common conduct exists;
6. mediation for disputes involving uncertain similarity or negotiated licensing;
7. arbitration for contractual disputes where the parties have agreed to it;
8. court proceedings for injunctions, damages, account of profits, statutory damages, or punitive remedies where available.

Mediation can be faster and less expensive than litigation, particularly where the dispute concerns a commercially useful design that can be licensed or modified. Arbitration can protect confidential model information and coordinate a contract dispute across borders, but it cannot bind a non-signatory rights holder and does not guarantee easy enforcement of an injunction in every jurisdiction. The supplied evidence does not establish a tested, interoperable cross-border arbitration framework for fashion-AI disputes.

Collective enforcement is essential. The Netherlands’ WAMCA procedure shows how representative organizations can pursue mass claims and damages, although AI claims may face individualized questions about which works entered a dataset, whether they were reproduced, and what each creator lost. In the United States, the Giana complaint shows why class treatment may be necessary where individual claims are too small to litigate. Neither example supplies a completed fashion-AI payout result.

### Remedies by type of wrong

| Wrong | Most appropriate first response | Possible final remedies | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unauthorized training on identified works | Disclosure, licensing negotiation, collective claim, regulator inquiry | Licence, remuneration, damages, injunction, deletion or retraining where technically possible | Proving ingestion and causation is difficult |
| Output reproduces a print, image, or garment design | Takedown, production pause, evidence preservation | Injunction, damages, account of profits, royalty, product withdrawal | Functional features and common trends may be unprotected |
| Style imitation without copying a work | Commercial-use restriction, attribution correction, identity or brand claim | Passing off, trademark, publicity, privacy, personality-right remedy where available | A general personal style should not become a copyright monopoly |
| Watermark or authorship removal | Takedown and preservation of original metadata | Copyright, moral-right, unfair-competition, or contractual remedy | Metadata may be missing or altered before discovery |
| AI-only output claimed as human-authored | Corrected disclosure and revised registration or contract | Limited or no copyright in the AI-only material; protection for human contributions | Human-contribution thresholds vary |
| Brand or supplier sells a copied output | Immediate stop-sale and supplier investigation | Damages, profits, injunction, recall, contractual indemnity | Contractual indemnity does not erase third-party liability |
| Model or likeness replicated without consent | Removal, identity-right notice, contract enforcement | Privacy, publicity, passing off, personality-right or consumer remedy | Coverage varies sharply by jurisdiction |

### Collective licensing and remuneration: feasible but not proven at scale

The policy debate often treats licensing as either impossible or sufficient. Both positions are too simple.

Licensing is feasible for curated archives, specialist fashion datasets, high-quality retrieval collections, fine-tuning data, and identifiable designers whose work has clear commercial value. The U.K. House of Lords reports that a licensing market is emerging, but that most public deals involve large rights holders and large developers. Smaller creators may be invisible in the market.

Collective licensing can solve scale. A collective body can aggregate independent designers, establish standard terms, process metadata, audit use, and distribute payments. But it creates risks:

- creators may not understand what they authorized;
- publishers or intermediaries may capture most of the value;
- a blanket licence may include creators who did not consent;
- per-work payments may be impossible to calculate for enormous datasets;
- the collective may lack bargaining power against a dominant developer;
- rights in prints, photographs, garment designs, models, and brands may belong to different parties.

A creator-first model should therefore require explicit and intelligible terms, transparent deductions, audit rights, minimum shares for primary creators, and an option for direct licensing where appropriate. For mass datasets, remuneration may need to combine a base access fee, usage tiers, revenue sharing, or a sectoral fund. These are policy designs, not established payout formulas. No supplied source demonstrates which formula produces fair or measurable fashion payments.

Retrospective compensation is harder than future licensing. A developer may not know which of millions of images were used, and a rights holder may not know whether a model memorized or merely learned a general pattern. Possible routes include negotiated settlement funds, collective claims, levies, or damages based on a reasonable royalty. Any such mechanism must avoid paying for abstract styles or public-domain ideas and should distinguish proven use from generalized market harm.

### Proportionality, feasibility, and cost

The burden falls unevenly. The U.K. Impact Assessment reports that 93% of creative-industry firms are micro businesses and that 77.8% have turnover below £250,000. It also reports that 70% of identified U.K. AI firms are micro businesses, 15% small, and 9% medium. A rule that requires each small designer to monitor the web or each small developer to clear billions of works would entrench large incumbents rather than protect creativity.[U.K. Impact Assessment](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/report-and-impact-assessment-on-copyright-and-artificial-intelligence/copyright-and-artificial-intelligence-impact-assessment)

A proportionate framework should therefore use differentiated duties:

- large general-purpose model providers should maintain detailed source and compliance records;
- specialized fashion platforms should disclose model scope, data practices, and output restrictions;
- small developers using licensed or public-domain datasets should receive clear templates and safe compliance pathways;
- independent designers should receive free or low-cost provenance, registration, and notice tools;
- regulators and collective organizations should provide shared auditing and enforcement services;
- downstream brands should bear stronger clearance duties when they manufacture and sell at scale.

The precise implementation cost is unavailable. The U.K. government expressly states that its evidence base is incomplete and that its options assessment does not monetize costs and benefits. There are no supplied empirical tests showing how licensing, provenance, or opt-out systems affect fashion innovation, access, or diversity.

### Avoiding overprotection

Protection must target identifiable rights and economic harm rather than every resemblance. Fashion depends on shared references, public-domain materials, cultural exchange, parody, criticism, trend participation, and independent discovery. An exclusive right over “minimalist tailoring,” “romantic florals,” “deconstructed denim,” or a broad designer style would impede rather than support creative diversity.

The *Rothy’s v. Giesswein* design dispute illustrates why resemblance is not enough. The registered-design case succeeded, but the unregistered design claim failed because copying could not be shown; similar recycled-plastic knit material could have been independently encountered by the defendant.[Cambridge fashion-IP analysis](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/fashion-and-intellectual-property/barriers-to-enforcing-design-rights-over-fashion-in-the-united-kingdom/9F6783E4C1E6A5EA0A430193C75CA13C)

The same principle should govern AI. A model producing a common silhouette should not automatically infringe. A generated print that reproduces an independent designer’s registered artwork, a model that outputs a distinctive protected composition after a targeted prompt, or a brand that falsely suggests endorsement presents a stronger case.

New style or personality protections should be narrow and carefully defined. They should target commercial exploitation, false endorsement, unauthorized replicas, or harmful deceptive uses while preserving satire, parody, biography, criticism, news, and transformative expression. The legal system should not use copyright to solve every problem caused by market substitution or cultural devaluation.

### Interoperability and model removal

Interoperable technical standards should use a shared vocabulary for:

- creator and rights-holder identity;
- asset identity and version;
- permitted purposes;
- training, fine-tuning, retrieval, evaluation, and display;
- territory and duration;
- remuneration terms;
- attribution requirements;
- withdrawal and deletion requests;
- output provenance and human contribution.

C2PA, RSL, TDMRep, robots.txt, fingerprints, watermarks, and registries can work together, but no one standard currently guarantees that a model will honor a designer’s preference. Metadata may be stripped, crawlers may be unidentified, datasets may be copied, and training may already have occurred before a reservation is registered.

Removal must therefore be divided into three different requests:

1. **Future access prevention:** stop a crawler or platform from collecting the work in later training.
2. **Dataset deletion:** remove the work from a stored dataset or private fine-tuning corpus.
3. **Model-level unlearning:** alter an already trained model so that it no longer retains or produces a work.

The first two can sometimes be implemented contractually or technically. The third is much harder. The supplied evidence contains no reliable, interoperable real-world model-level removal system with audited results. A policy should not promise that an opt-out automatically erases historical model influence.

## 7. Bottom-line assessment and remaining uncertainties

AI fashion-design tools are not yet proven to be causing industry-wide creative homogenization. The evidence supports a more precise conclusion: they can narrow collective variation in particular workflows while increasing individual access, speed, and experimentation. The strongest convergence mechanisms are concentrated training data, shared prompts, interface defaults, commercial ranking, and weak human re-authoring. The strongest countervailing mechanisms are culturally curated data, visual exploration interfaces, multi-tool workflows, technical fashion expertise, and deliberate human selection and reconstruction.

The copyright disputes can be resolved only by separating the questions. Training-data authorization is not the same as output copying. Output copying is not the same as style imitation. Human authorship is not the same as provider permission. Attribution is not the same as ownership. A contract between a designer and a platform is not a defence against every third-party claim.

The most defensible settlement is a licensing-first, provenance-supported, human-centered model:

- license training, fine-tuning, retrieval, and commercial uses where the applicable law requires permission;
- use collective licensing and creator-first remuneration for mass uses;
- require meaningful transparency, with public summaries and confidential granular records;
- preserve provenance through signed metadata, fingerprints, watermarks, and interoperable rights signals;
- record human creative decisions and disclose AI assistance;
- conduct human output clearance before commercial manufacture;
- allocate responsibility among developers, platforms, brands, users, and suppliers by control and benefit;
- provide rapid takedowns, production pauses, mediation, collective claims, and proportionate damages;
- protect specific expression, designs, brands, and identities without granting monopolies over trends or general styles;
- impose stronger obligations on large model providers while keeping compliance accessible to independent designers and small firms.

Several uncertainties remain material. There is no representative longitudinal fashion study that measures AI-assisted output diversity across brands and cultures. There is no fashion-only meta-analysis separating body, material, cultural, and aesthetic convergence. The four jurisdictions lack a settled set of binding training and output precedents. The treatment of virtual garments, AI-generated patterns, and digital fashion remains incomplete. No supplied source demonstrates a proven collective licensing system that reaches independent fashion designers with measurable payouts, a reliable model-level removal mechanism, or a cross-border mediation and arbitration framework that has been tested in fashion disputes.

Those gaps do not justify abandoning the analysis. They explain why the present answer must be conditional. AI can make fashion more accessible and more experimental, but it can also make the industry more repetitive when the same data, language, defaults, and market incentives govern everyone’s search for novelty. The legal response should protect identifiable creative labor and give independent designers practical bargaining power without turning every shared aesthetic into private property.
